title: Kamarajar and Jawaharlal Nehru: Renouncing Power for Public Service — The Kamaraj Plan (1963)
summary: In 1963, K. Kamaraj stunned the nation by proposing that senior ministers, including himself as Chief Minister, resign from office to serve the common people—a historic move known as the Kamaraj Plan.
keywords: Kamarajar and the Hungry Cowherd: 'Close the File, Feed the Child!' — 1956
full_text:
In the shadow of the 1962 border conflict, India faced deep political turbulence. Inside the ruling party, factional infighting and careerism were eroding the grassroots idealism that had fueled the freedom struggle.

Distressed by the creeping cynicism in national politics, the Chief Minister of Madras State, K. Kamaraj, traveled to New Delhi with a daring proposal for Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.

Kamaraj spoke with disarming directness:
"Panditji, our leaders have become too comfortable in ministerial offices. Official cars, bungalows, and executive power have detached us from the common people in the villages. The only way to restore the moral authority of the movement is for senior leaders to step down from government and return to full-time grassroots service among the masses!"

Nehru looked at Kamaraj with both admiration and skepticism:
"It is a noble vision, Kamaraj. But who among our established leaders will willingly surrender high office?"

Without an instant's hesitation, Kamaraj replied with characteristic humility:
"I will begin, Panditji. I hereby submit my resignation as Chief Minister of Madras. A leader must demonstrate sacrifice before asking others to follow!"

True to his word, Kamaraj resigned. His selfless example sparked an unprecedented wave across the nation: six senior Union Cabinet ministers—including Lal Bahadur Shastri, Morarji Desai, and Jagjivan Ram—along with six state Chief Ministers tendered their resignations to undertake organizational work.

In the history of democratic politics, the 'Kamaraj Plan' stands as an extraordinary monument to the principle that public office is not an entitlement, but a temporary instrument of selfless service.

moral: A true leader does not cling to power; they possess the moral courage to relinquish high office to serve the common good.
